techniques.T1003: t1003 os credential dumping adversaries attempt to extract credentials from operating system caches, memory, or on-disk data structures such as the sam database, lsass process memory, or the active directory database (ntds.dit). credentials are typically recovered in hash or plaintext form and used for lateral movement, privilege escalation, or persistence via pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, or offline cracking. each sub-technique below targets a distinct extraction surface: process memory, an on-disk credential database, a registry secret store, or the flat credential files that mirror these same primitives on linux. lsass (local security authority subsystem service) a protected windows process (lsass.exe) that authenticates logons and holds the resulting credential material — ntlm hashes, kerberos tickets, and in older/misconfigured setups even reversible or plaintext secrets — in memory for the duration of a session. it is the single highest-value memory target on any windows host, which is why t1003.001 exists as its own sub-technique. credential material types ntlm hash (a fixed hash of the password, reusable directly via pass-the-hash without ever knowing the plaintext); kerberos ticket / tgt (a time-bound token that can be replayed via pass-the-ticket, or a krbtgt hash that can forge new tickets — a golden ticket); dcc2 / mscache v2 (a salted, iterated hash of a domain logon cached for offline use — cannot be pass-the-hash'd, only cracked offline); plaintext (recoverable only if wdigest or a similar legacy provider is enabled, or from an application that mishandles secrets in memory). sam vs ntds.dit the sam (security account manager) database holds *local* accounts for a single machine, at %systemroot%\system32\config\sam. ntds.dit is its domain-wide equivalent — the full active directory database, living only on domain controllers — and dumping it exposes every domain account at once, not just one host's local accounts. registry hive a hive is an on-disk file backing a section of the windows registry. sam, system, and security are each separate hive files; system holds the boot key needed to decrypt secrets in the other two, which is why adversaries almost always export all three together with reg save rather than just one. privilege levels required most of these sub-techniques need system or local-administrator rights on the target host (t1003.001–.005, .007, .008). dcsync (t1003.006) is different: it needs no code execution on a domain controller at all, only an account holding the replicating directory changes / replicating directory changes all ad permissions — normally domain admins, enterprise admins, and dc computer accounts. object access auditing (sacl) windows does not log handle or read access to files and registry keys (security 4656/4663) by default — it requires an explicit system access control list on the object plus the "audit object access" policy enabled. most of the file/registry-based detections in this guide only produce telemetry if this auditing was deliberately turned on beforehand; verify it's enabled before relying on those event ids in your own environment. volume shadow copy (vss) a windows service that creates a point-in-time snapshot of a volume. files that are normally locked while in use by the os — like an active ntds.dit — can be read freely from a shadow copy, which is why vssadmin create shadow shows up repeatedly in ntds and sam extraction procedures as a way around file locks. drs / drsuapi replication protocol the rpc interface domain controllers use to replicate directory data with each other. dcsync works by calling this same interface from a non-dc host and asking a real dc to "replicate" account data to it — the dc has no way to tell the request isn't coming from a legitimate peer dc, which is why the defense is access-control on who holds replication rights, not the protocol itself. /proc filesystem (linux) a pseudo-filesystem that exposes live kernel and process state as if it were files. /proc/<pid>/maps shows a process's memory layout; /proc/<pid>/mem is a direct read/write window into that same memory. root can read any process this way, making it the closest linux equivalent of dumping lsass. /etc/passwd vs /etc/shadow /etc/passwd is world-readable and holds account metadata only (no hashes since the shadow-password scheme replaced inline hashes decades ago). /etc/shadow holds the actual password hashes and is root-only (mode 0600) by default — the two files must be combined (e.g. with unshadow) before offline cracking tools can use them.
techniques.T1558: t1558 steal or forge kerberos tickets adversaries subvert kerberos authentication by stealing or forging tickets to enable pass the ticket. kerberos realms involve three parties — a client, a service, and a key distribution center (kdc) that issues the tickets after authentication. depending on which credential material an adversary already holds (the krbtgt hash, a service account's hash, or simply the ability to make requests as an authenticated user), they can forge a ticket that impersonates any account, forge one scoped to a single service, brute-force a legitimately-issued ticket offline, or lift a ticket straight out of a running session's credential cache. windows ships a built-in `klist` utility for listing and inspecting cached kerberos tickets. the three kerberos actors and two ticket types a client authenticates once to the kdc's authentication service (as) and receives a ticket granting ticket (tgt) — proof of domain authentication, encrypted with the krbtgt account's key. from then on, the client presents that tgt to the kdc's ticket granting service (tgs) to request a service ticket (tgs) for whatever specific resource it wants to reach, and that service ticket is encrypted with the target service account's own key, not krbtgt's. this tgt-vs-tgs split is exactly why golden tickets (which need krbtgt's hash) and silver tickets (which need one service account's hash) are forged differently and have very different blast radii. spn (service principal name) an spn is what binds a kerberos service ticket request to a specific service account — every service running under a domain account (sql server, iis app pool, etc.) registers one. by protocol design, any authenticated domain user can request a tgs ticket for any registered spn, no special privilege required. that's not a bug — it's how kerberos normally works — but it's also the entire precondition that makes kerberoasting possible: an attacker just has to ask, then try to crack what comes back. encryption types (etype): rc4 vs aes kerberos tickets are encrypted with one of several negotiable algorithms. rc4-hmac (etype 23 / 0x17) derives its key directly from the account's ntlm hash and is unsalted, which is exactly why an rc4-encrypted service ticket can be brute-forced offline straight back to a crackable hash. aes128/aes256 (etype 17/18) use a stronger, salted key derivation that resists this. a domain that has fully moved to aes-only kerberos meaningfully raises the cost of both kerberoasting and as-rep roasting — which is why 'unexpected rc4 in an aes-enforced environment' is one of the most reliable detection signals across this whole technique family. kerberos pre-authentication pre-authentication requires the client to encrypt a timestamp with its own key before the kdc will issue a tgt — proof the client actually knows the password, not just that it knows the username. it exists specifically to prevent an attacker from requesting as-rep data for an arbitrary username and cracking it offline. some accounts have it explicitly disabled (a legacy interoperability setting some applications historically needed), and that setting is the entire precondition for as-rep roasting. pass-the-ticket vs. pass-the-hash t1558 sits one layer up the credential-material stack from t1003: a stolen ntlm/dcc2 hash (t1003) still has to be exchanged for a ticket at some point to reach a kerberos-authenticated resource, whereas a stolen or forged ticket (t1558) skips that exchange entirely and can be replayed directly. that's also why several t1558 sub-techniques are direct payoffs of a t1003 dump — krbtgt's hash from t1003.003/t1003.006 becomes a golden ticket here. ticket lifetime as a forgery tell a standard active directory domain's default domain policy caps a tgt's lifetime at 10 hours ("maximum lifetime for user ticket"). forging tools default to far longer validity unless an operator deliberately overrides it — a multi-day or multi-year ticket lifetime on a 4769 event is one of the more reliable golden-ticket tells precisely because matching the legitimate default takes extra, easy-to-forget effort on the attacker's part.
techniques.T1059: t1059 command and scripting interpreter adversaries abuse the command and script interpreters built into nearly every platform to execute commands, scripts, and binaries. these aren't attacker tools — they're the os and its applications doing exactly what they were built to do, which is what makes this technique family so hard to blanket-block and so dependent on behavioral, contextual detection rather than simple allow/deny lists. the 13 sub-techniques below cover the major interpreters an adversary might reach for, from powershell and cmd.exe on windows through unix shells, python, javascript, and visual basic, out to network device clis, cloud apis, hypervisor shells, and container orchestration tooling. why this whole technique family is dual-use by design every interpreter covered here — powershell, bash, python, cmd.exe — is a legitimate, necessary part of the system it runs on. nothing about launching one is inherently malicious. that means detection here can't be about the binary's existence; it has to be about intent signals: what argued it, what it did next, whether the command line is obfuscated, whether the parent process makes sense. this is the single biggest mindset shift from a technique like t1003, where the mere presence of certain artifacts (a lsass dump file, a dcsync replication request from a non-dc) is itself a strong signal. living-off-the-land (lolbins) and why allowlisting alone fails most of these sub-techniques use binaries that are already present on the system by default — powershell.exe, cmd.exe, python (if installed), wscript.exe, osascript. an application-control policy that just blocks 'unknown' executables does nothing here, because nothing about these binaries is unknown or unsigned. this is why mitigations across this whole family lean on execution-prevention policies (constrained language mode, script signing, denylisting specific interpreters where they're not operationally needed) rather than generic allowlisting. in-memory script execution vs. file-based av a script interpreter can execute code that never touches disk as a file — piped in via `-command`, downloaded and `invoke-expression`'d directly, or run from a string in a scheduled task. traditional file-scanning antivirus has nothing to inspect in that case. this is exactly why windows added powershell module logging (event id 4103) and script block logging (event id 4104) to the powershell operational log — they capture what the interpreter actually executed, not just that it launched, closing the visibility gap file-based scanning leaves open. interpreter choice is about availability, not unique capability for an attacker, powershell, python, and a unix shell are largely interchangeable — pick whichever is already present and least likely to be flagged in that specific environment. a defense built around blocking one interpreter ("we disabled powershell") routinely gets sidestepped by simply switching to python, vbscript, or javascript instead, which is why several sub-techniques below exist as near-equivalents to each other rather than as a strict hierarchy of sophistication. encoding and obfuscation as the near-universal tell base64-encoded powershell (`-encodedcommand`/`-enc`), string concatenation to break up flagged keywords, char-code-built strings in javascript, obfuscated vba — this pattern repeats across nearly every interpreter covered here. it's one of the single highest-value generic signals in this whole technique family: legitimate administrative scripts are very rarely deliberately obfuscated, so a genuinely encoded or heavily obfuscated command line is disproportionately likely to be worth a look regardless of which interpreter carried it.

subtechniques.T1003.001: t1003.001 lsass memory the local security authority subsystem service (lsass) holds credential material generated during user logon in process memory. with administrative or system-level access, an adversary can open a handle to lsass.exe and either harvest credentials in-memory or dump the process to disk for offline analysis with tools like mimikatz. common execution paths include mimikatz's sekurlsa module, sysinternals-style procdump, the built-in comsvcs.dll minidump export invoked through rundll32.exe, and abuse of windows error reporting (silent process exit) to trigger a crash dump of lsass on demand. why lsass holds credentials at all: the ssp architecture at startup lsass loads a set of security support provider (ssp) dlls — msv1_0.dll (ntlm), kerberos.dll (kerberos), wdigest.dll (wdigest), tspkg.dll/livessp.dll (terminal services/live sso) — and each one keeps its own copy of credential material in memory so the user isn't re-prompted for a password on every authentication (single sign-on). sekurlsa::logonpasswords in mimikatz simply walks each ssp's internal memory structures and prints what it finds; it isn't exploiting a bug, it's reading data lsass is deliberately keeping around for sso. why some dumps show a plaintext password wdigest, one of those ssps, historically kept a reversibly-encrypted copy of the plaintext password (needed to answer http digest auth challenges). since windows 8.1 / server 2012 r2, and via kb2871997 on backported older systems, the registry value hklm\system\currentcontrolset\control\securityproviders\wdigest\uselogoncredential defaults to 0, which stops wdigest from caching it. a lsass dump that yields plaintext almost always means this value was explicitly set back to 1, or the host predates the patch. the grantedaccess mask is the actual fingerprint to read another process's memory, a caller needs a handle to it obtained via openprocess() with specific access rights (process_vm_read, process_query_information, etc.), and windows encodes exactly which rights were granted as a bitmask. sysmon 10 logs that mask verbatim as grantedaccess — values like 0x1010 or 0x1fffff aren't arbitrary detection strings, they're the literal access rights a credential-reading tool needs, which is why they're such a reliable signal. why file-based and api-based dumping produce the same result mimikatz's in-memory reading and the comsvcs.dll/procdump file-dumping route both ultimately rely on the same os capability: a full memory snapshot of lsass.exe (via minidumpwritedump in dbghelp.dll, or equivalent direct memory reads). once a .dmp file exists, it can be moved off-box and parsed offline with mimikatz's minidump module with no live access to the original host required — this is why detecting the dump file's creation matters as much as detecting the initial process-access. how protected process light (ppl) actually stops this credential guard and ppl work by marking lsass.exe itself as a protected process in the kernel. once protected, even an administrator-token process's openprocess() call against it is rejected outright by the kernel unless the calling process is itself signed and running as a protected process of equal or higher level — this is a kernel-enforced access check, not something a normal admin tool (including most dumping utilities) can bypass, which is why m1025/m1043 are the mitigations that actually change the threat model rather than just adding detection. sandworm team used the plainpwd mimikatz variant and rundll32.exe + comsvcs.dll to dump lsass. hafnium deployed procdump against exchange servers to harvest credentials post-compromise. volt typhoon targeted hashed credentials from lsass memory as part of a living-off-the-land intrusion set. cobalt strike injects into or reads lsass memory to extract password hashes via its built-in mimikatz integration. mimikatz sekurlsa::minidump and sekurlsa::logonpasswords modules parse lsass memory for plaintext credentials and hashes. sysmon 10 (processaccess) targetimage = lsass.exe with a grantedaccess mask indicative of full or memory-read rights (e.g. 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1fffff, 0x143a). security 4656 / 4663 handle requested / object access attempt on lsass.exe — requires object-level sacl auditing enabled on the process, not on by default. sysmon 1 / security 4688 process creation for rundll32.exe with comsvcs.dll and minidump on the command line, procdump.exe, or task manager's dump-file helper. sysmon 11 (filecreate) .dmp / .mdmp file creation in non-standard paths shortly after a lsass handle event. lsass memory access (defender for endpoint) kql flags processes opening lsass with access rights consistent with credential dumping, excluding common legitimate callers. lsass dump via comsvcs.dll minidump sigma catches the built-in-binary lolbin path for dumping lsass: rundll32.exe invoking comsvcs.dll's undocumented minidump export. lsass dump via comsvcs.dll minidump (cortex xdr) xql cortex xdr equivalent of the comsvcs.dll minidump lolbin detection. mimikatz credential common fallback path. t1558.003 kerberoasting a frequent follow-on once an attacker has working credentials: request service tickets for offline cracking rather than touching lsass again. t1550.002 subtechniques.T1003.002: t1003.002 security account manager the sam database holds local account credentials, normally enumerable only via apis like net user. with system-level access an adversary can extract it in-memory or export the underlying registry hives (hklm\sam, hklm\system) with reg save for offline parsing by tools such as creddump7. local rid 500 is the built-in administrator, rid 501 is guest, and rid 1000+ are regular local accounts — the values attackers are actually after. why system is required, and why reg save still works the sam hive's registry key acl restricts read access to the system account only, and the file backing it is exclusively locked while windows is running. reg save doesn't need to break that lock — it asks the registry subsystem itself (a kernel-mode api) for a consistent copy, which is why it works even while the os is fully up, but it still fails without system-equivalent rights because the acl check happens regardless of the access method. syskey and why system must be exported too hashes inside the sam hive are not stored in the clear — they're encrypted with a per-machine boot key (introduced by the syskey feature in nt4 sp3) that is itself scattered across obfuscated values in the system hive. sam alone is unusable ciphertext; every real-world extraction (mimikatz, secretsdump.py, reg save scripts) grabs sam and system together specifically because system supplies the key that unlocks sam offline. why ntlm hashes are worth stealing directly unlike the salted dcc2 hashes covered under t1003.005, local ntlm hashes are unsalted — the same password always produces the same hash. that means a stolen ntlm hash doesn't need to be cracked at all; it can be replayed directly against any service that accepts ntlm authentication (pass-the-hash), which is why local sam extraction is often a lateral-movement enabler even without ever recovering a plaintext password. apt28 executed reg save against sam, system, and security hives during the nearest neighbor campaign. wizard spider acquired credentials from the sam and security registry hives. crackmapexec dumps usernames and hashed passwords directly from sam. impacket (secretsdump.py) extracts sam hashes both locally and remotely via registry hive retrieval. iceapple credential dumper module reads encrypted password hashes from hklm\sam\sam\domains\account\f and the users subkeys. security 4656 / 4663 handle/access events on hklm\sam — requires sacl auditing configured on the hive, not default. sysmon 1 / security 4688 reg.exe with save and a target of hklm\sam, hklm\system, or hklm\security on the command line. sysmon 11 (filecreate) .save / .hiv / .dmp files created by reg.exe or a copy command shortly after the reg save. sam/system/security hive dump via reg.exe kql flags reg.exe save commands targeting the three registry hives commonly exported for offline sam cracking. sam/system/security hive dump via reg.exe (cortex xdr) xql cortex xdr equivalent of the reg.exe save detection. sam/system/security registry hive dump via reg.exe sigma vendor-agnostic version of the same reg.exe save pattern. scheduled backup/imaging jobs (windows server backup, third-party agents) that export registry hives as part of routine system-state backup documented it disaster-recovery hive exports verify whether the account/process has an authorized change ticket for hive export check for exfiltration of the resulting .sav/.hiv files (archive creation, outbound network transfer) if compromise is confirmed, rotate local administrator passwords across any host sharing the same local admin password (deploy/verify laps) search for follow-on pass-the-hash using the extracted local hashes against other hosts m1027 password policies enforce pulled from sam are unsalted and directly reusable via pass-the-hash against hosts sharing the same local admin password.
subtechniques.T1003.003:
t1003.003 ntds ntds.dit, normally at %systemroot%
tds
tds.dit on a domain controller, is the active directory database and holds credential material for every domain account. adversaries extract it via ntdsutil.exe's install from media (ifm) function, by creating a volume shadow copy of the dc's volume and lifting the file directly, or remotely via impacket's secretsdump.py over the drsuapi replication interface (which overlaps functionally with dcsync). it's an ese/jet database, not a proprietary format ntds.dit is built on the extensible storage engine (ese, also called jet blue) — the same database engine exchange uses for mailbox stores. that's why generic ese tooling like esentutl.exe can interact with it directly, and why offline parsers (impacket's ntds parsing, dsinternals) can walk the same well-documented table structure rather than reverse-engineering something bespoke. why volume shadow copy is the standard workaround like the sam hive, ntds.dit is held open exclusively by the ntds.exe/lsass.exe service the entire time the dc is running, so it can't simply be copied. vss solves this the way it solves it for any backup software: it creates a block-level, point-in-time snapshot of the whole volume, and files are read from that snapshot rather than the live, locked file — the copy operation never touches the actual in-use handle. two layers of encryption, same pattern as sam values inside ntds.dit are encrypted with a password encryption key (pek) that is itself stored in the database but wrapped by the boot key from the dc's own system registry hive. this mirrors the sam/system relationship exactly, which is why every real ntds extraction — ntdsutil ifm, secretsdump, manual vss copy — always grabs the system hive alongside ntds.dit; without it the database is just encrypted bytes. ifm is a legitimate feature being repurposed ntdsutil's "ifm" (install from media) mode is a real, microsoft-documented way to stand up a new domain controller without full network replication — it packages a consistent snapshot of ntds.dit plus the system hive specifically so a new dc can be seeded offline. the abuse in this sub-technique isn't a flaw in ifm; it's using a legitimate provisioning feature for its side effect (a portable, ready-to-decrypt copy of every credential in the domain) rather than its intended purpose. lapsus$ used the built-in ntdsutil.exe to extract the ad database. scattered spider extracted ntds.dit by creating volume shadow copies of virtual domain controller disks. apt28 used ntdsutil.exe and vssadmin-created shadow copies during the nearest neighbor campaign. volt typhoon used ntdsutil to build dc installation media containing usernames and hashes. impacket (secretsdump.py) dumps ntds.dit contents remotely via the drsuapi interface or from an offline copy. sysmon 1 / security 4688 ntdsutil.exe with "ac i ntds" / "ifm" arguments, or vssadmin.exe create shadow, or esentutl.exe invoked against the ntds volume. security 4663 file access events on %systemroot%

subtechniques.T1003.004: t1003.004 lsa secrets lsa secrets, stored under hkey_local_machine\security\policy\secrets, hold credential material windows itself needs at boot before a user logs on — commonly service account passwords, scheduled task run-as credentials, and cached rdp/auto-logon passwords. system-level access lets an adversary export the key with reg.exe or pull it from memory with mimikatz's lsadump::secrets. why windows needs a credential store nobody has logged into yet some things windows must do before any human authenticates: start services configured to log on as a specific account, run scheduled tasks under a stored run-as identity, resolve an auto-logon password, or apply the machine account's own password for domain communication. none of those can wait for a user-specific decryption key, so windows keeps this narrow set of secrets in a location lsa can decrypt to itself at boot — that location is exactly hklm\security\policy\secrets. same boot-key protection as sam and ntds lsa secrets values are encrypted with a key derived from the same system-hive boot key that protects sam and ntds.dit. a raw reg save of the security hive alone yields ciphertext — the exporting tool still has to perform the boot-key-derived decryption offline, which is exactly what mimikatz's lsadump::secrets module (and equivalents in impacket/gsecdump) automates. why this is often a lateral-movement multiplier because lsa secrets frequently holds service-account passwords, and the same service account is commonly reused across many machines in an environment, one host's lsa secrets dump can hand over credentials with reach far beyond that single box — unlike a local sam dump, which is scoped to that machine's local accounts. apt29 used reg save for offline lsa secret extraction. lazagne harvests credentials directly from lsa secrets. impacket (secretsdump module) obtains account and password information from lsa secrets. threat group-3390 used gsecdump to dump lsa secrets and domain controller credentials. aadinternals dumps secrets from the local security authority, including hybrid-identity-relevant material. security 4656 / 4663 handle/access events on hklm\security\policy\secrets — requires a sacl on the key. sysmon 1 / security 4688 reg.exe save targeting hklm\security, or execution of lazagne / gsecdump / mimikatz. sysmon 10 (processaccess) mimikatz reading lsa secrets in-process alongside its usual lsass memory access. lsa secrets registry access kql flags non-lsass reads of the lsa secrets key; lsass itself reads this constantly and must be excluded to avoid flooding. reg.exe save targeting security hive (cortex xdr) xql cortex xdr process-creation equivalent, catching the reg.exe save path to lsa secrets rather than the registry-read event itself. lsa secrets registry access (non-lsass) sigma same logic in sigma form for sysmon registryevent telemetry. lsass/system itself legitimately reads this key continuously — must be filtered out or the rule is unusable password vault/pam agents configured to resolve service-account secrets through supported apis rather than raw registry export identify which service-account secrets were exposed — accounts configured for scheduled tasks/services on that host are the likely targets rotate every service-account credential that was stored on that host subtechniques.T1003.005: t1003.005 cached domain credentials windows caches the last several domain logons (dcc2 / mscache v2 hash format) at hkey_local_machine\security\cache, under subkeys nl$1 through nl$10, so users can still log on when a domain controller is unreachable. mimikatz's lsadump::cache module or the cachedump tool extract these; unlike ntlm hashes, dcc2 cannot be pass-the-hash'd directly and requires offline cracking. on linux, ad-integrated hosts running sssd or quest authentication services keep an equivalent cache at /var/lib/sss/db/cache.[domain].ldb or /var/opt/quest/vas/authcache/vas_auth.vdb. why the cache exists: offline logon a laptop that's off the corporate network — no domain controller reachable — still has to let a user log in with their normal domain password. windows solves this by caching a derived hash of each of the last several successful domain logons locally, and only consults it when no dc responds. how dcc2 is actually derived dcc2 isn't a simple hash of the password. windows first computes the standard nt hash (md4 of the utf-16le password) as an intermediate value (this intermediate is what's historically called dcc1), then runs that through pbkdf2 with hmac-sha1, using the lowercased username as the salt and 10,240 iterations, keeping the first 128 bits of the result as dcc2. the username-as-salt means the identical password produces a different hash for every account, and the 10,240-round pbkdf2 makes each guess roughly two to three orders of magnitude slower to test than a raw ntlm hash. why it can't subtechniques.T1558.003: t1558.003 kerberoasting any authenticated domain user can request a tgs ticket for any registered service principal name — that's normal kerberos behavior, not a misconfiguration. when the returned ticket is rc4-encrypted, the encrypted portion is effectively the service account's ntlm hash used as a key, making it crackable offline with no further access to the network required. an attacker just requests tickets for every spn they can enumerate, takes them offline, and lets a cracking rig grind against them. why any user can trigger this — it's not a permission bug kerberos is designed so that requesting a service ticket doesn't require any special right beyond being an authenticated domain user with a valid tgt — the kdc's job is to issue the ticket, not to decide whether you should be allowed to try authenticating to that service. authorization happens later, at the service itself. that means kerberoasting isn't exploiting a flaw; subtechniques.T1059.013: t1059.013 container cli/api docker and kubernetes both expose a full-featured api (dockerd, the kubernetes control-plane api server) that their respective clis (docker,
